newsitem.title: USA: Taped brutality draws FBI probe of Texas prison.
newsitem.headline: Taped brutality draws FBI probe of Texas prison.

text.p: In another U.S. controversy mixing law enforcement and charges of racism, a civil rights investigation was opened on Tuesday into a Texas prison where guards videotaped prisoners being brutalized, the FBI said.

The graphic tape was likely to raise new questions about some prison systems in the United States, much as the beating of black motorist Rodney King by white police -- caught on videotape in California six years ago -- caused an uproar over police tactics.
"There is an alleged civil rights violation investigation ongoing at the Brazoria County Detention Center" south of Houston, FBI spokesman Rolando Moss said.

The tape made by guards there during a drug raid nearly one year ago showed prisoners being forced to crawl. One attacked by a dog howled; another with an injured ankle was shot in the buttocks with a stun gun.
Because of the tape, officials in Oklahoma and Missouri were removing some 700 prisoners from Texas prisons where they had bought space to ease overcrowding in their own systems.

Missouri, which was bringing back 415 prisoners from the privately run Brazoria facility, canceled a $6 million contract it had to house prisoners there and was considering legal action to recover money for breach of contract.
A spokesman for Missouri Gov. Mel Carnahan said the state was reviewing its contracts with Texas prisons, where hundreds of prisoners have been housed under rental agreements.
Chris Sifford, Carnahan's press secretary, said "we are also considering legal action" against the operators of the Brazoria County prison to be reimbursed for money spent.
The Missouri Department of Corrections said temporary quarters were being created in prison gymnasiums and elsewhere for the prisoners being brought back from the Brazoria prison.
By Tuesday 200 Missouri convicts had been returned, and another 215 were to be brought back in a few days. About 700 other Missouri prisoners were housed in several other Texas institutions.
Oklahoma began transferring more than 250 of its inmates out of a different Texas facility operated by Capital Correctional Resources Inc., the company that runs the prison where the tape was made.

Officials at the Brazoria prison said the guards made the tape as a "training film" to demonstrate "what not to do" to quell a prison uprising, adding that the allegations of abuse had been blown out of proportion.

The United States has about 1.7 million prison beds, and private companies operate about 85,000 beds in local, state and federal prisons. But the private companies are quickly building market share. They accounted for 20 percent of the 100,000 beds added last year.
The Justice Department reported earlier this month that in 1995 federal prisons held 24 percent more inmates than their rated capacity and state prisons were 3 percent overfilled.
